title: Two caravans
hookLine: one leader trusts spirits who say to throw away the water; the other keeps it (Jataka 1)

lines: WET CLOTHES, MUD ON THE WHEELS.
cards: Why haul all those heavy jars? There's plenty of water ahead, pools and lakes.
The travelers who say it come down the desert road looking like people just out of a rainstorm: wet clothes, lotus flowers in their hair, mud on their cart wheels. They're friendly.
Throw the water out, they say, and move faster. In the first tale of the Jataka, two caravans meet travelers like these. One leader listens.

teach.b: First, the two leaders. Both are merchants about to cross the same desert. One is the bodhisatta, the future Buddha.
The other is a young man the tale calls foolish, eager to go first for the best grass and water. The bodhisatta lets him.
Second, the first caravan. Deep in the desert, the friendly travelers appear: a demon and his followers in disguise. The young leader believes them.
His people pour their water onto the sand, walk on, find no pools at all, and by night they're too weak to resist. The demons devour the caravan. Third, the second caravan.
The bodhisatta meets the same strangers and the same advice. He doesn't argue or panic.
He reasons. There's no rain wind blowing, no storm cloud on the horizon, and this desert is known to be dry. And these people's eyes are red and they cast no shadow, the tale says.
So he tells his caravan: not one drop is to be thrown away until we see new water with our own eyes. They walk on, pass the bones of the first caravan, and cross safely. Fourth, the point.
The tale doesn't praise suspicion for its own sake. It praises checking what's in front of you before trading away what keeps you alive. Advice wearing all the right costumes can still be wrong.

how: The Apannaka Jataka stands first in the Pali Jataka collection, and Buddhist teachers tell it as a lesson in thinking a situation through before acting on persuasive advice.

o: two kings racing to cross the same desert
one trusts a disguise, one checks the sky
a merchant trading water for safe passage

p: went first and poured out the water
kept every drop until new water
a demon and his followers in disguise
no rain wind, no storm cloud

s: the bodhisatta's caravan went first across the desert
he let the young merchant go first, and followed later.
the strangers looked as if they'd just come out of the rain
wet clothes, lotus flowers, mud on the wheels: the whole costume was a trick.
the tale teaches that every stranger is an enemy
it praises checking what's in front of you before you give up what keeps you alive.

games.q: you're leading a caravan across a dry desert. friendly travelers with wet clothes say there's water ahead and you should pour yours out to move faster. what do you do?
o: pour it out. they've clearly just seen rain.
keep every drop until you see new water yourself.
pour out half, to be safe both ways.
games.why: the bodhisatta notices no rain wind and no storm cloud, keeps the water, and his caravan crosses safely past the bones of the one that listened.

practice: Name one plain thing that keeps you steady: sleep, a walk, ten minutes without your phone.

Notice the voices that say drop it, you're too busy, there'll be plenty later, and look at the sky the way the bodhisatta did: is there really rain ahead? Then let a quiet decision settle, to keep the jar full.

wordCard.voice: Two caravans. One pours out its water on a stranger's word; one checks the sky and keeps it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali apannaka, the name of this first tale; translators render it as something sure or certain.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the water. The week in lines: verses sung from memory, a line of your own, the songs closed, then the Jataka: who was who, a vow in the mud, ten perfections, two caravans. That's day eight hundred nineteen.
